name: STM32WBA54KGU6
title: Arm Cortex-M33 100 MHz wireless MCU with Bluetooth LE and IEEE 802.15.4 radio, up to 1 MB flash, 128 KB SRAM, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: The STM32WBA5 family pairs a 100 MHz Arm Cortex-M33 (TrustZone, FPU, DSP, MPU) and an 8 KB instruction cache with a 2.4 GHz radio for Bluetooth LE, and on the WBA54 and WBA55 also IEEE 802.15.4 (Thread, Matter, Zigbee), reaching +10 dBm out and -96 dBm sensitivity at 1 Mbps. Members carry 512 KB or 1 MB of ECC flash and 96 KB or 128 KB of SRAM, a 2.5 Msps 12-bit ADC, two comparators, touch sensing, two I2C, two SPI, two USARTs, an LPUART and a SAI, plus AES, a DPA-resistant SAES, PKA, HASH and a true random generator. The core runs from an internal LDO, or on the WBA55 from an internal step-down converter, on a single 1.71 V to 3.6 V supply. The STM32WBA54KGU6 is the 1 MB WBA54 in the 5 x 5 mm UFQFPN32, rated -40 to 85 °C ambient.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, FPU, DSP and MPU, up to 100 MHz, 410 CoreMark
Up to 1 MB flash with ECC (256 KB rated 100k cycles), up to 128 KB SRAM, 512-byte OTP
2.4 GHz Bluetooth LE 6.0 and IEEE 802.15.4; +10 dBm max output in 1 dB steps; -96 dBm (BLE 1 Mbps), -97.5 dBm (802.15.4 250 kbps)
Rx 4.4 mA, Tx 0 dBm 5.2 mA typ at 3.3 V (SMPS)
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; LDO on all parts, SMPS step-down on WBA55
Stop 1 6.5 µA (SMPS, 3.3 V), Standby with SRAM1 retained 0.93 µA (SMPS, 3.3 V), Standby 0.16 µA (1.8 V), typ at 25 °C
3.35 mA typ at 100 MHz on SMPS, 6.16 mA on LDO, 3.3 V
12-bit 2.5 Msps ADC (up to 16 bits by oversampling), two comparators
UFQFPN32 5 x 5 mm, UFQFPN48 7 x 7 mm, WLCSP41 2.76 x 2.98 mm, UFBGA59 5 x 5 mm

operation.text: The WBA52 (CE, CG, KE, KG) has Bluetooth LE only, no SAI, no comparators, no PTA or external PA control. The WBA54 (KG, CG, KE, CE) adds IEEE 802.15.4, PTA, external PA control, AoA/AoD, one SAI and two comparators, with the core supplied by the LDO. The WBA55 (CG, CE, HG, UG, UE) is the WBA54 with the SMPS step-down converter added. G parts have 1 Mbyte flash and 64 KB SRAM1; E parts 512 Kbytes and 32 KB SRAM1. SRAM2 is 64 KB on all.

Arm Cortex-M33 at up to 100 MHz with the Armv8-M main extension: TrustZone secure and non-secure states, single-precision FPU, DSP instructions, MPU with up to 16 regions per state, and an SAU of up to eight regions. It fetches code over its C-AHB bus and data over its S-AHB bus. Benchmark: 410 CoreMark (4.10 CoreMark/MHz).

An 8 KB cache on the C-AHB bus gives zero wait states on a hit and allows execution from flash at 100 MHz without stalls on hits. It is two-way set associative by default (pseudo-LRU replacement), or direct mapped to save power, with hit-under-miss, critical-word-first refill, separate master ports to flash and SRAM, hit and miss counters, and four remappable regions that extend caching beyond code space.

A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix links the CPU and GPDMA1 to flash, SRAMs and peripherals. GPDMA1 has eight channels with linked-list programming, four priority levels (one high-priority queue), peripheral and memory transfers in every direction, byte reordering, packing and padding, and TrustZone and privilege separation per channel. Channels 0 to 5 have an 8-byte FIFO, channels 6 and 7 a 32-byte FIFO. It keeps running in Sleep and Stop 0.

Up to 1 Mbyte in 8-Kbyte pages, with ECC (single-error correction, double-error detection, failing address reported) and an optional 128-bit prefetch. Endurance is 10000 cycles over the whole array and 100000 cycles on 32 pages (256 Kbytes). A 512-byte OTP area (32 rows) holds user data. Two write-protected areas of 8-Kbyte granularity can be set. With TrustZone on, a watermark sets a secure area, a hide-protection area (HDP) at its start can be locked against all access until the next reset, and each page can be marked secure or privileged on the fly.

RDP has levels 0, 0.5 (TrustZone only: secure area closed to debug), 1 (flash closed to debug, RAM boot and bootloader; regression to lower levels can need a password) and 2 (debug, RAM boot and bootloader disabled). Level 2 is permanent unless a secret key was set beforehand, in which case it can be taken back to level 1 by password through JTAG/SWD. Going from level 1 to 0 erases flash, backup registers and SRAMs.

SRAM1 (up to 64 KB) and SRAM2 (64 KB with parity) can each be powered down in Stop mode and either can be kept in Standby. Both serve peripherals working autonomously. With TrustZone on they start secure and can be split secure/non-secure and privileged/unprivileged in 512-byte blocks through the MPCBB.

The boot address comes from the BOOT0 level (pin PH3, or an option bit when the pin is freed for GPIO), the nBOOT0 and nSWBOOT0 option bits and the NSBOOTADDx or SECBOOTADD0 option bytes. Targets: any user flash address, the system bootloader, embedded SRAM, or the RSS. The factory bootloader programs flash over USART, I2C or SPI. With TrustZone on, boot must be in the secure area, and BOOT_LOCK forces every boot to SECBOOTADD0. The RSS, in a secure information block, provides secure firmware installation (SFI) once TrustZone is enabled.

After reset the CPU is secure, the SAU marks all memory secure, SRAMs and MPCBB are secure, all GPIOs and all interrupts are secure, securable and TrustZone-aware peripherals are non-secure, the block-based flash area is non-secure, and illegal-access interrupts are off. The GTZC (TZSC, TZIC, MPCBB) sets the security and privilege of peripherals and memories.

The radio covers Bluetooth LE 1 Mbps coded and 1 Mbps and 2 Mbps uncoded GFSK, and on the WBA54 and WBA55 IEEE 802.15.4 at 125 kbps and 250 kbps, with concurrent operation. It supports direction finding (AoA/AoD) with antenna switch control (RF_ANTSW0 to 2), external PA control (RF_EXTPABYP), packet traffic arbitration, a sleep timer, and runs from one 32 MHz crystal. VDDRFPA sets the reachable output power. On LDO packages VDDANA is bonded to VDDRF inside; on QFN packages VSSRF is the exposed pad. Regulatory targets: FCC part 15, IC RSS-139 and RSS-210, ETSI EN 300 328, EN 300 440 and EN 301 489-17, ARIB STD-T66.

Packet traffic arbitration with co-located radios such as WiFi, after IEEE 802.15.2: grant and deny signalling over one to four wires (PTA_ACTIVE, PTA_PRIORITY, PTA_STATUS, PTA_GRANT), programmable polarities and timing, and transmit abort.

VDD (1.71 V to 3.6 V) feeds the I/Os, regulators, reset, power management, internal clocks and backup domain. VDDA (1.62 V to 3.6 V with the ADC) feeds the ADC and comparators and is tied to VDD or, unused, to VSS. VDDSMPS (SMPS packages) and VDDRF go to the same supply as VDD. VDDRFPA and VDDANA may range from 0 to 3.6 V but sit at 1.2 V or more for the radio to run and never above VDDRF; VDDANA may be fed from VDD11. VDDHPA takes 470 nF.

An LDO and an SMPS sit in parallel to make VCORE for logic, SRAMs, radio and flash. The LDO output is on VCAP with 4.7 µF typical; the SMPS output is on VDD11 with 4.7 µF typical in total, reached through a 2.2 µH inductor from VLXSMPS. The device can move between SMPS and LDO while running, and both regulators work in Stop modes and support two voltage ranges. An SMPS device used with the LDO only and no inductor has VDDSMPS and VLXSMPS grounded.
Range 1 sets VCORE to 1.2 V for CPU and peripherals up to 100 MHz; range 2 sets 0.9 V for up to 16 MHz, with the radio unavailable. AHB5 is limited to 32 MHz in range 1 and 12 MHz in range 2.

While VDD is below 1 V, the other supplies (VDDA) stay below VDD + 300 mV; from 1 V up they are independent. On power-down VDD may briefly fall below the other supplies only while the energy delivered to the device stays under 1 mJ, which lets decoupling capacitors discharge at different rates.

A brown-out reset runs in every mode and holds the device in reset while VDD is below its threshold, so no external reset circuit is needed; the lowest level, used at power-on, is 1.71 V, and higher levels are chosen by option bytes. A programmable voltage detector, enabled by software, compares VDD with a selectable threshold and raises an interrupt on crossing it. In Stop 1 and Standby the BOR can sample in an ultra-low-power mode (ULPMEN).

Run starts after reset. Sleep stops only the CPU. Stop 0 keeps the main regulator on for the fastest wake-up and the most active peripherals; Stop 1 runs on the low-power regulator, keeps SRAM and registers, and allows fewer peripherals. In both, VCORE clocks, PLL, HSI16 and HSE32 stop while LSE or LSI run, and the system restarts on HSI16. Standby turns the core domain off; SRAM and registers are lost except the backup domain, unless SRAM1, SRAM2 or the radio are kept on the low-power regulator (Standby retention). I/O levels can be held with pull-up, pull-down or floating. Standby ends on NRST, IWDG, a WKUP pin edge, an RTC event or a tamper, and also on the sleep timer when the radio is retained.

In Stop 0, ADC4, LPTIM1/2, USART1/2, LPUART1, SPI1/3, I2C1/3, the radio (range 1 only) and GPDMA1 work without the CPU; in Stop 1 the same peripherals except the radio and GPDMA1 keep working and can call up Stop 0 to move data with GPDMA1. Each asks for its kernel clock, and HSI16 as system clock when it needs DMA, only while it needs them, can be started by hardware triggers, and can wake the device. Typical uses: timer-triggered ADC sampling with wake-up on an analog watchdog, I2C/SPI/UART transfers, sensor polling, and GPIO driven from SRAM.
During and after reset the I/Os are in analog state with the Schmitt trigger off, and the reset pull-up is switched off when the reset source is internal. All GPIOs start in analog mode.

SYSCLK comes from HSE32 (32 MHz crystal or external clock, software trimmable), HSI16 (16 MHz RC, ±1% factory trimmed) or a PLL of up to 100 MHz fed from either; the PLL has three independent outputs and can also clock the ADC and the RNG. Low-speed sources: LSE (32.000 or 32.768 kHz crystal with selectable drive, or bypass), LSI1 (32 kHz, ±5%, can be divided by 128 to 250 Hz, clocks the IWDG) and LSI2 (32 kHz, ±500 ppm, can clock the radio sleep timer). The device starts on HSI16. An HSE32 failure switches SYSCLK to HSI16; an LSE failure switches to LSI. MCO outputs an internal clock in Run, Sleep and Stop, and LSCO outputs LSI or LSE in every mode. AHB and APB run up to 100 MHz, AHB5 up to 32 MHz.

Each pin can be push-pull or open-drain output, input with or without pull-up/down, alternate function or analog. Most pins are 5 V tolerant. Configurations can be locked. GPDMA1 can drive GPIOs in Stop 0. Pins can be made secure individually. Up to 35 I/Os depending on package.

The NVIC handles up to 72 maskable vectors plus the 16 core vectors with 16 priority levels, banked for secure and non-secure states. The EXTI routes I/O and peripheral events to interrupts, events and wake-up from Stop, with edge selection, software triggers and secure inputs.

One 12-bit successive-approximation ADC at up to 2.5 Msps (0.4 µs per 12-bit conversion), selectable 12, 10, 8 or 6 bits, oversampling up to x256 for up to 16-bit results, self-calibration, three analog watchdogs, single, continuous, scan and discontinuous modes, software or hardware triggers, DMA, wait and auto-off modes, and autonomous operation down to Stop 1. Up to 19 multiplexed channels: up to nine external inputs plus the temperature sensor, VREFINT and VCORE. Input range VSSA to VDDA; supply 1.62 V to 3.6 V; ADC clock 140 kHz to 55 MHz after its prescaler. VSSA connects to the VSS pin. VREF+ connects to VDDA inside. A calibration after each power-up is advised, and below VDDA = 2.4 V the I/O analog switch booster is used.

The source resistance RAIN in front of an analog pin is limited by resolution and sampling time. The pin also sees Cparasitic, the PCB plus pad capacitance; a large Cparasitic lowers accuracy, which a lower fADC recovers. The pin leakage Ilkg adds to the error.

VSENSE rises linearly with temperature and is read on an ADC4 channel. The offset differs from part to part, so uncalibrated it suits only relative measurements. Each device carries factory readings at 30 °C (TS_CAL1) and 130 °C (TS_CAL2), and a VREFINT reading at 30 °C (VREFINT_CAL), all taken at VDDA = 3.0 V and stored in read-only system memory.

Two rail-to-rail comparators with a selectable reference (VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of it, or an external pin), programmable hysteresis, speed/power mode and output polarity. They can wake the device from Stop 0 and Stop 1, raise interrupts, feed timer break inputs, and pair up as a window comparator.

Surface charge-transfer capacitive sensing for keys, sliders, wheels and proximity: up to 20 channels (count depends on package), up to six acquired in parallel, one sampling capacitor serving up to three channels, spread spectrum, programmable charge frequency and maximum count, and end-of-acquisition and error interrupts.

The RNG delivers 32-bit true random words from an analog source with a NIST SP800-90B conditioning stage and health tests, four words every 412 AHB cycles below 77 MHz. AES and SAES implement FIPS 197 with ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM, GMAC and CCM for 128- or 256-bit keys; SAES resists DPA, can use the hardware-derived key (DHUK), the boot key (BHK) or their XOR, and can pass a key to the faster AES. One 128-bit ECB block takes 51 cycles (AES) or 528 cycles (SAES) with a 128-bit key. HASH computes SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, MD5 and HMAC. The PKA accelerates RSA, DH and ECC over GF(p) with DPA protection. A 96-bit unique ID and a CRC unit are included.

TIM1: 16-bit advanced control timer, four channels, three complementary outputs with dead time, for three-phase PWM. TIM2 (32-bit) and TIM3 (16-bit): up/down counters with four channels and quadrature encoder support. TIM16, TIM17: 16-bit up counters with one channel and one complementary output, combined into IRTIM for an infrared LED. LPTIM1, LPTIM2: 16-bit low-power timers that run in Stop mode from HSI16, LSE, LSI or an external clock and can wake the device. Two SysTick timers (secure and non-secure).

The IWDG has a 12-bit down counter and prescaler, runs from LSI in Stop and Standby, and is started by hardware or software through option bytes. The WWDG has a 7-bit down counter clocked from the APB clock with an early warning interrupt.

The RTC is a BCD calendar with sub-seconds, two alarms, a 17-bit wake-up timer, timestamp, 0.95 ppm digital calibration and reference clock input; it runs from LSE, LSI or divided HSE32 and keeps going in every low-power mode on LSE or LSI while VDD is present. TAMP has 32 backup registers kept by VDD, up to six external tamper pins (passive, or active with outputs shared over up to four inputs), nine internal tamper sources, and erases backup registers, SRAM2, ICACHE and crypto state on detection.

Two I2C (I2C1, I2C3): controller and target, Sm 100 kbit/s, Fm 400 kbit/s, Fm+ 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive, 7- and 10-bit addressing, SMBus 3.0 and PMBus 1.3, independent kernel clock, analog and digital filters, DMA, and autonomous work in Stop with wake-up. The SDA and SCL pins are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDD is switched off but still present.

USART1 and USART2 support asynchronous, synchronous master/slave, smartcard (ISO 7816), IrDA, LIN, Modbus, RS-485 driver enable, auto baud, 8-byte FIFOs and up to 20 Mbaud. LPUART1 runs up to 9600 baud from the 32.768 kHz LSE so it can wait for data in Stop mode, and faster from a faster clock. All three work autonomously in Stop with DMA and wake-up.

SPI1 is the full instance (4- to 32-bit data, 16 x 8-bit FIFOs, CRC 5 to 33 bits); SPI3 the limited one (8- or 16-bit data, 8 x 8-bit FIFOs, up to 1024 data per transfer). Both do master and slave, Motorola and TI formats, hardware NSS, an optional RDY handshake pin, DMA, and autonomous work in Stop with wake-up.

One serial audio interface with two sub-blocks, each transmitter or receiver with an 8-word FIFO: I2S, LSB/MSB justified, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC'97, SPDIF out and PDM, 8- to 32-bit data, up to 16 slots, master or slave.
SWJ-DP gives JTAG or two-wire SWD; TMS/SWDIO and TCK/SWCLK are shared, and a sequence on TMS selects the port. JTAG pins not used can be GPIOs.

Each supply pair (VDD, VDDA, VDDRFPA, VDDRF against VSS) gets ceramic capacitors placed at or under its pins: 100 nF per VDD pin plus 10 µF, 100 nF plus 1 µF on VDDA, 100 nF on VDDRF, VDDRFPA and VDDANA, 470 nF on VDDHPA, 4.7 µF on VCAP or VDD11, and 10 µF on VDDSMPS. VDD and VDDRF come from the same supply.
IDD figures are the total device current into VDD, VDDA, VDDRF, VDDRFPA and VDDSMPS where present, or for radio figures the current into VDDRF and VDDRFPA.

The 32 MHz crystal oscillator has an internal programmable capacitor bank (6.6 pF to 23.6 pF in steps of about 270 fF) that trims the crystal frequency and offsets PCB parasitic capacitance. The crystal is specified for the NX2016SA and NX1612SA references. Bluetooth LE needs ±50 ppm total tolerance after trimming. An external 32 MHz clock may be AC coupled through 470 pF to 100 nF.

The 32.768 kHz crystal and its load capacitors sit as close to OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT as possible to keep distortion and start-up time down. No resistor goes between the two pins. Drive strength is set by LSEDRV, and the crystal's critical Gm must stay below the Gmcritmax of the chosen drive. In bypass mode the oscillator is off and OSC32_IN takes an external clock as a standard input.

An input held at an intermediate level draws current through its Schmitt trigger, and a floating input can pick up noise. Unused pins are left in analog mode, or given a defined level with a pull resistor or by setting them as outputs. ADC inputs are set to analog mode. A pulled input driven to the opposite level draws current through its pull resistor.
Each I/O sinks or sources up to ±8 mA, or ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH. The sum of I/O currents plus the device's own current stays within ΣIVDD and ΣIVSS.

NRST has a CMOS input with a permanent pull-up RPU. A 0.1 µF capacitor at the pin, close to the device, guards against parasitic resets. Any external reset source has to pull NRST below VIL(NRST) max or the reset is not seen.
PB15 and PH3 handle signals up to 16 kHz, and PC14 and PC15 up to 250 kHz, with OSPEED left at low speed on these pins.

Firmware should handle a corrupted program counter, unexpected resets and corrupted control registers. Holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 second reproduces most common failures for pre-qualification, and ESD can then be applied directly to check that the software recovers.
